function.name: glob
function.description: Fast file pattern matching tool that works with any codebase size. It supports glob patterns and returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

function.name: grep
function.description: A powerful search tool built on ripgrep. Prefer Grep when you know the exact symbols or strings to search for. Returns 'path:line: text' matches by default.

path.description: optional file or subdir to limit the search

glob.description: optional glob to filter files, e.g. '*.py'

-A.description: lines of context after each match

-B.description: lines of context before each match

-C.description: lines of context before and after

function.name: read
function.description: Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool. Returns numbered lines.

offset.description: the line number to start reading from (1-indexed, optional)

limit.description: the number of lines to read (optional)

function.name: scope
function.description: Enclosing function or class of a line, with its span, signature and docstring.

function.name: definition
function.description: Where a symbol is DECLARED, as opposed to everywhere it appears. Returns every candidate declaration with its file and line; reports none rather than guessing when the symbol is imported, generated or defined in a dependency.

function.name: refs
function.description: Every place a symbol appears in the repository, grouped by file.

function.name: analogues
function.description: Sibling code that does the same job as this file -- same directory, shared naming stem -- and which decorators each sibling carries that this file does not. A missing access check often exists in the peer that does the same job.

function.name: entrypoints
function.description: Where untrusted input can enter a file: routes, handlers, event listeners, CLI.

function.name: origin_of
function.description: Where the values used on a line came from -- walks backwards through the enclosing function and labels untrusted sources (request, environment, event payload). Local to one function; a parameter stops the chain.

function.name: cwe_info
function.description: MITRE CWE description, abstraction level, parents and concrete child weaknesses.

steps.message:
You are localizing a vulnerability, starting from ONE file that has already been chosen for you. CITE WHERE THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY IS. If the deciding lines are in the file you were given, cite them there. If your evidence says they are in another file, cite that file by its real path and say why -- a correct citation elsewhere is worth more than an approximate one here, and it is scored on the path you name.
Do not pad. A line you cannot justify is not a hedge, it is a wrong answer that dilutes a right one.
NEVER USE GLOB. The file is already chosen -- finding files was the previous stage's job and it is finished. A glob here is you re-running a search that is already over.
LOOK wherever the evidence leads, though, with the tools below. They read the whole repository on purpose -- a value arrives from a caller, a guard lives in the sibling that does the same job, a symbol is declared three directories away -- and none of them glob. Following those is how you find the right LINE. What you must not do is start a fresh search for a different file to answer about instead: follow evidence out of the file, do not go looking for somewhere better to answer.
If the weakness is really in another file, say so and cite it THERE. Naming the right line in the right file is the answer; the closest line in this one is not a fallback, it is a worse answer.
Your tools, and what each one answers:
- cwe_info(cwe) returns the MITRE description, abstraction level, and the parents and concrete children WITH their descriptions. Worth ONE call when the weakness label is a Class or Pillar -- those name no mechanism to look for, and the children do. Do not call it again on a child: you already have that text. The advisory wording in the question is more specific than any Class-level description, so prefer it.
- entrypoints(path) lists where untrusted input can ENTER this file -- routes, handlers, event listeners, CLI. Start here: a line is only exploitable if something outside can reach it.
- origin_of(path, line) walks BACKWARDS from a line to where its values came from, and in python follows the chain into the CALLERS when it ends at a parameter -- those hops are where the input usually arrives. Labels untrusted sources. CALL IT on every line you are about to cite, before you cite it. When the chain reaches an untrusted source, cite where that value ARRIVES or where the missing check belongs, not the later line where the effect is visible. If the chain stops at a parameter, say so and cite the parameter -- that is an answer, not a failure.
- scope(path, line) returns the enclosing function with its exact bounds and signature.
- definition(symbol) returns where a symbol is DECLARED, with file and line -- not every place it appears. Use it before citing a line for a symbol you have not read: it reports NOTHING rather than guessing when the symbol is imported or defined elsewhere, and that is the answer.
- refs(symbol) lists every use site of a symbol, grouped by file.
- analogues(path) lists files doing the SAME JOB as this one -- same directory, shared naming stem -- and the decorators each carries that this file does not. When a guard is missing here, the sibling that does the same job usually has it; read the difference, do not assume what it means.
- grep(pattern, path, glob, output_mode) searches file CONTENTS. Anchor it: a bare word across a repository returns the vendored copies first. Skip compiled and generated files -- a .js.map or a bundled dist/ is the same code with the names stripped, and matching it tells you nothing you could cite.
- read(path, offset, limit) returns numbered source. THE RESULT IS CAPPED, so a large limit does not return a large file -- you get the first part and a note saying what was cut. Read the region you need rather than paging a whole file from the top.
Cite the SPAN A CORRECTIVE PATCH WOULD REPLACE -- the statement and whatever must change with it. Not one line lifted out of a larger change, and not a whole function wrapped around one statement.
Put ONE citation on each line. Never write several line numbers on the same line.
Give an optional explanation (max 50 words), then your citations inside a <final_answer> tag, e.g.:
<final_answer>
path/to/file.py:41-46 (one clause saying why these lines are the weakness)
path/to/file.py:88 (a second location, if there is one)
</final_answer>
